title: When One Modality Is Not Enough:Multimodal Sex and Life-Stage Classification of Red Deer from Aerial RGB–Thermal Video

paper.title:
When One Modality Is Not Enough: Multimodal Sex and Life-Stage
Classification of Red Deer from Aerial RGB–Thermal Video
paper.abstract: Abstract Aerial drone surveys increasingly support wildlife population estimation, yet a useful census is more than a count: population dynamics are defined by species composition, sex ratios and age structure, that is, by which species are present and how a herd splits into adult males, adult females and juveniles. We use red deer ( Cervus elaphus ) as a test case, because managers act on these dynamics and because the visible cue defining adult males, the antlers, is seasonally variable. Surveys are flown nadir, the cameras looking straight down while the drone flies high enough not to disturb the animals, so each deer occupies only a small, low-resolution patch. The two recording modalities fail in opposite conditions: in color a deer under canopy blends into the ground, while in thermal it becomes a bright blob that loses fine detail. Rather than trust either modality alone, we fuse them at every stage using self-supervised DINOv3 features. Our pipeline tracks animals in both modalities, treats an animal as confirmed only when the two cameras agree, keeps only the clear, non-occluded frames, and assigns species and sex by a vote across them; life stage is read separately from geo-referenced body size, since at survey resolution a juvenile often only differs from an adult female in size. Across four flights spanning the antler season the fused pipeline correctly classifies 25 of the 26 detected individuals (7 of 8 adult males, all 16 adult females and 2 juveniles), against 20 of 26 for either sensor alone. The multimodal species classification reaches 96.0 % 96.0\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} , while for the sex classification, the fusion of the two sensors matters most: the combined RGB+thermal model is the most robust across environments and seasons. Automating the demographic classification turns a drone flight from a count into a repeatable reading of herd structure, so the sex ratios and age structure that managers already act on can be gathered as often as a survey can be flown.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Wildlife management needs to know not merely how many animals are present but which animals: how a population divides into adult males, adult females and juveniles. A survey reads that composition as a snapshot, the age and sex structure from which recruitment, survival and population trend are afterwards estimated [ 7 ] , yet it is exactly what detection and counting models do not report. We study the problem on red deer ( Cervus elaphus ), where the male/female/juvenile split is a standard management variable and the cues are unusually well defined from above: adult males carry antlers and adult females do not, while juveniles can look like small adult females and are difficult to tell apart by appearance at survey resolution. Uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) make repeated, low-disturbance surveys practical [ 13 , 9 ] , and pairing an RGB with a thermal camera is attractive in forest habitats, where animals slip in and out of canopy and its shadow. The two modalities fail in opposite conditions: in RGB a deer in cast shadow or under a crown is almost indistinguishable from the background, while in thermal it is an unmistakable bright blob but fur color is lost and antlers are visible only seasonally, limited by low resolution and warm-ground clutter. Figure 1 shows both failures, and which sensor performs better depends on the time of year: in June the velvet antlers are still warm and resolve in thermal, while by September they have hardened and gone thermally dark, so the cue survives only in RGB. Figure 1 : Why one modality is not enough, and why it is seasonal. One test area, two flights, each an RGB | | thermal pair with the male enlarged. In A1 (September) the antlers have hardened and gone thermally dead, so the sex cue survives only faintly, and only in RGB. In A2 (June) deer resting in the shaded strip beside the barn are barely separable from the ground in RGB but bright in thermal, where the warm velvet antlers resolve.

sections.heading: From rejecting cases to selecting frames.
sections.text: Prior work on the same data treated the demographic label as a question of ecological evidence as much as of modeling: on small, occluded nadir crops the sex cue is often simply absent from a given view, so the response is to abstain rather than guess [ 23 ] . It also showed that heads built on pretrained foundation-model representations beat smaller specialized architectures such as YOLO, whose weaker capacity struggles with the faint cues of aerial imagery. Abstaining matters because forcing ambiguous crops into a class injects label noise that corrupts the classifier [ 28 , 12 ] , and clean supervision here is usually bought through active learning and review [ 19 , 20 ] . But abstention has a price: rejected crops are often ambiguous animals, and a census cannot discard its hard cases. In video an animal is not one crop but a track of many frames across the two modalities, so we reject the frames on which the evidence is absent or limited and settle sex and life stage by voting over the survivors, which keeps the clean-label benefit without losing the individuals abstention would discard. No single modality and no single frame is therefore enough for an individual-level census, yet almost all aerial wildlife pipelines stop at detection, counting or coarse tracking and leave the demographic step to manual review. We close that gap for one species as a demonstration that the step can be automated at all. The work extends a thermal-only localization and tracking pipeline [ 32 ] from one thermal stream to paired RGB–thermal detection and cross-modal tracking, from the native camera perspective to terrain-orthorectified imagery, and from localization to demographic classification. On the public BAMBI dataset ( Sec. 3.1 ) we contribute a pipeline that fuses the sensors at every stage and outputs, per individual, a species, a sex call, a life-stage flag and an occlusion-aware confidence, rendered onto the tracked video.

sections.heading: Scope and questions.
sections.text: Four questions run through what follows. (i) What does cross-modal confirmation buy when deciding which tracks are animals and which are sensor noise ( Secs. 3.2 and 2 )? (ii) Which modality carries the sex signal ( Secs. 3.3 and 5 )? (iii) Does selecting frames rather than classifying all of them sharpen the census ( Secs. 3.3 and 4 )? (iv) How reliable is a box-derived size cue as a life-stage biometric, and what limits it ( Secs. 3.3 and 5 )?

sections.heading: 2.1 Aerial wildlife datasets and fine-grained interpretation
sections.text: Two things separate our setting from most airborne wildlife work: the habitat is forested rather than open, and the output is a demographic profile rather than a count. Airborne monitoring has mostly been developed for open habitats, where animals are comparatively visible and RGB alone often suffices for localization, counting and tracking [ 13 , 9 , 27 ] . Recent methods cut annotation effort further by learning density-based localization from points rather than boxes [ 5 ] , but do not recover the extent, orientation or appearance that individual tracking and demographic analysis need. Under canopy, RGB–thermal fusion improves robustness [ 2 , 21 ] , and thermal UAV surveys support red deer counting [ 39 ] and antler-based sex-ratio estimation [ 16 ] . All of these return aggregate quantities: a count for a flight, or a single ratio for a herd. None attaches a species, a sex and a life stage to an individual animal, and it is that step, from a population-level summary to a per-animal record, that we take here.

sections.heading: 2.2 Tracking and re-identification
sections.text: Online trackers of the SORT family [ 1 ] pair a constant-velocity Kalman filter [ 18 ] with greedy association and remain a strong, simple baseline for aerial video. Appearance re-identification increasingly rests on self-supervised features: DINOv2 and DINOv3 [ 29 , 35 ] give transferable descriptors without labels, which triplet metric learning [ 34 , 15 ] can sharpen for identity and attribute discrimination. In ecology such metric learning underpins animal photo-identification [ 25 ] , though careful evaluation is needed to separate real gains from tuning artifacts [ 26 ] . Tracking alone does not scale to a survey: stitchers assume a static landscape, so animals that move during a flight are duplicated or ghosted in the orthomosaic and bias the count, which is why removing duplicates by distinguishing individuals is named an open direction [ 3 ] , while thermal UAV work on ungulates stops at detection and counting [ 31 , 39 ] . Aerial re-identification is usually approached from a lateral view, at least for species whose markings sit on the flank: Sun et al . [ 36 ] pair YOLOv11 with a DINOv2 pose classifier but maneuver the drone around each animal to expose it. Of the 53 53 datasets in WildlifeDatasets / MegaDescriptor [ 4 ] only AerialCattle2017 uses nadir views, because for cattle their coat pattern makes them separable. Red deer carry no such marking apart from the males’ antlers, which makes nadir re-identification harder.

sections.heading: 2.3 Selective prediction and frame quality
sections.text: When evidence is weak it is often better to abstain than to force a label; selective classification formalizes this reject option [ 6 , 11 ] , and modern variants pair a classifier with a confidence estimate that decides when to defer [ 12 , 14 ] . These are general formulations rather than wildlife methods; the one treatment on aerial wildlife imagery we know of is the prior work on this same red deer data [ 23 ] . Here the analogous decision is which frames to classify at all , since an occluded or badly posed crop carries no reliable demographic evidence, and forcing it into a class injects label noise [ 28 ] . That work abstains per frame; we move the principle to the track level ( Sec. 3.3 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Data and evaluation protocol
sections.text: We use the matched and orthographic subsets of the public BAMBI dataset [ 33 ] ( https://github.com/bambi-eco/Dataset ): paired, undistorted RGB–thermal recordings from temperate Austrian forests and forest edges, flown nadir with DJI M3T/M30T drones at 30 m to 60 m 30\text{\,}\mathrm{m}60\text{\,}\mathrm{m} above ground. RTK multi-GNSS gives centimeter-level per-frame pose, so each frame can be used in the native camera perspective or re-projected onto the terrain as an orthophoto (“geo”), in which detections carry world coordinates. The dataset ships bounding-box tracks , each with a species and, where identifiable, sex and age, plus an occlusion flag on the key frames. Red deer ( Cervus elaphus ) is the richest demographic class: 1613 1613 tracks and 26 674 26\,674 key frames, with sex annotated on 41.0 % 41.0\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of tracks, age on 67.6 % 67.6\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} and an occlusion flag on 49.5 % 49.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of key frames. Tracks and frames without a given label are unused by the corresponding head.

sections.heading: Three supervision sources.
sections.text: Species labels come from a multi-species crop set ( 653 653 roe deer, 6868 6868 red deer, 4698 4698 wild boar paired crops). Occlusion labels are the per-key-frame visibility flags, giving 20 531 20\,531 labeled crops ( 14 744 14\,744 clear, 5787 5787 occluded). Sex follows the strictest protocol: every matched crop was re-reviewed independently by three annotators free to abstain, and only the 3908 3908 crops on which a majority agreed ( 556 556 male, 3352 3352 female/juvenile) were kept, so the sex head trains on a consensus-filtered set spanning the 2023–2024 antler cycle [ 23 ] , available at https://zenodo.org/records/21061638 .

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: Detectors are split by flight , every sixth flight held out, so no annotated track is shared between training and validation. Individuals need not be disjoint, since the same animal can appear on more than one flight of an area, but the model never sees a track twice. Classification heads are evaluated leakage-free with GroupKFold by animal track . The census pipeline is then evaluated on four further BAMBI flights, held out of every training set, from three test areas and denoted A1 , A2 (two flights over area A, three years apart), B and C . These are the flights for which we hold field-verified demographic ground truth, so a per-individual census can be scored against what was present. Each census comes from one flight alone, and we do not link individuals across flights. Species is predicted for every detected animal; sex and life stage only for red deer, the one class with enough demographic annotation to support them.

sections.heading: 3.2 Detection and cross-modal tracking
sections.text: Figure 2 gives the overall flow: the synchronized RGB and thermal (TH) streams are detected, tracked and cropped, then passed through a hierarchical classifier whose species and demographic stages run only on the frames an occlusion filter keeps. Rather than fuse the sensors at pixel level we fuse them in embedding space, so each supplies the cue it resolves best. Figure 2 : Overview of the hierarchical, multimodal pipeline. Animals are detected and tracked in RGB and thermal video and cropped; each crop then passes occlusion filtering, species classification and demographic classification, with frame-level predictions aggregated per track by majority vote.

sections.heading: Detection.
sections.text: A single-class ( animal ) YOLO26x [ 17 ] detector runs per modality at 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 ; for the orthographic tests the detectors are trained on content-cropped orthophotos instead (source 2048 2048 px, typically around 1200 1200 px after cropping) to avoid model-internal rescaling. At inference each panel is run at a deliberately low confidence, keeping every candidate in the pool 𝒟 m = { b : s ⁡ ( b ) ≥ τ det } \mathcal{D}_{m}=\{b:s(b)\geq\tau_{\text{det}}\} with τ det = 0.01 \tau_{\text{det}}=0.01 and m ∈ { RGB , TH } m\in\{\text{RGB},\text{TH}\} , where b b is a candidate box and s ⁡ ( b ) s(b) its detector confidence. This pool is not what we report as detections; it is revisited later to fill gaps inside tracks that are already established.

sections.heading: Thermal-anchored boxes.
sections.text: Once matched, the thermal box is taken as the reference size, being the looser of the two and so more reliably enclosing the whole animal, antlers included. The RGB box is redrawn at thermal size, anchored on the RGB centroid and refined by template matching as described by Praschl et al . [ 33 ] . Tracks are established from confident detections only ( s ⁡ ( b ) ≥ 0.2 s(b)\!\geq\!0.2 ); gaps are then filled from the pool 𝒟 m \mathcal{D}_{m} down to s ⁡ ( b ) ≥ τ det s(b)\!\geq\!\tau_{\text{det}} , snapping a low-confidence detection to the track when it lies near the position predicted from surrounding frames. Because a box is recovered only where a real detection supports it, none are hallucinated.

sections.heading: 3.3 Hierarchical demographic classification
sections.text: Tracks yield frames of uneven quality, and forcing every frame into a label injects noise that corrupts downstream classifiers [ 28 ] . Prior work on this data abstains on ambiguous crops [ 23 ] , but per frame , discarding each detection in isolation. We move the principle to the track , selecting only the frames worth trusting and aggregating across the survivors, so an animal is never discarded, only its unreliable frames are.

sections.heading: From raw embeddings to classification.
sections.text: Every crop is embedded once with frozen DINOv3 ViT-H+ features [ 35 ] in three input configurations : rgb ( 1280 1280 -d), thermal ( 1280 1280 -d) and combined ( 2560 2560 -d, the concatenation). Each head (occlusion, species, sex) maps its input onto a 256 256 -d embedding with its own triplet-trained projection ϕ \phi , then classifies that embedding linearly. With anchor a a , hardest positive p p and hardest negative n n , ϕ \phi is trained by batch-hard mining [ 34 , 15 ] , ℒ triplet = [ ∥ ϕ a − ϕ p ∥ 2 − ∥ ϕ a − ϕ n ∥ 2 + α ] + , \mathcal{L}_{\text{triplet}}=\big[\,\lVert\phi_{a}-\phi_{p}\rVert_{2}-\lVert\phi_{a}-\phi_{n}\rVert_{2}+\alpha\,\big]_{+}, (3) where ϕ x \phi_{x} is the projected embedding of crop x x , α \alpha the margin and [ z ] + = max ⁡ ( 0 , z ) [\,z\,]_{+}=\max(0,z) . Crucially, combined concatenates the two feature vectors before the projection, so the head learns a joint representation rather than combining two decisions. Reporting every stage for all three configurations isolates what each modality and their fusion contribute. The labels are read in a fixed order: occlusion, then species, then sex. The occlusion head labels every crop clear or occluded , and only the clear frames 𝒞 i \mathcal{C}_{i} of individual i i continue. On 𝒞 i \mathcal{C}_{i} the species head votes, and its majority call fixes the species; this can stand as the final answer when the evidence is too weak for a demographic call. Sex reuses exactly those frames. The sex head is binary, separating adult males from everything else, because the only cue visible from nadir is the antler: calves lose their natal spots within weeks, and thereafter a juvenile of either sex differs from an adult female only in size at this resolution. Its second class is therefore female / juvenile , split by size alone below. The head commits each clear crop f f to one class, giving a per-frame call s ^ f \hat{s}_{f} , and the individual’s sex is the majority call, y ^ i = 𝟏 [ ∑ f ∈ 𝒞 i 𝟏 [ s ^ f = male ] > 1 2 | 𝒞 i | ] \hat{y}_{i}=\mathbf{1}[\,\sum_{f\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\mathbf{1}[\hat{s}_{f}={\color[rgb]{0,0.59,0.9}\textbf{male}}]>\tfrac{1}{2}\lvert\mathcal{C}_{i}\rvert\,] . Voting is what makes a noisy per-frame call safe to use: the antler is resolved only from some angles, so many frames of a true male look female, but a male that resolves his antlers on more than half of his clear frames still carries the vote. This is where we depart from the per-frame treatment of the same data in prior work [ 23 ] , which adds a confidence band around the decision boundary and lets the uncertain middle abstain [ 6 , 12 ] . We place the reject decision at the occlusion stage instead: filtering removes the frames on which the evidence is physically absent, and the vote absorbs the rest, so no individual is ever abstained on. Sex leaves a juvenile inside the female / juvenile class, so life stage is recovered afterwards from body size. We switch to the orthorectified (“geo”) frames, whose box area is a metric body-size proxy, and restrict to the seasonal window in which adults and juveniles differ most. Because box tightness is not comparable between flights we compare only within a flight, taking each individual’s median track area a i a_{i} and flagging low outliers with a robust median-absolute-deviation (MAD) z z -score, z i = 0.6745 ​ a i − median j ⁡ a j MAD j ⁡ a j , z_{i}=0.6745\,\frac{a_{i}-\operatorname{median}_{j}a_{j}}{\operatorname{MAD}_{j}a_{j}}, (4) with the median and MAD taken over the individuals j j of that flight. Individual i i is called a juvenile only when both conditions hold: it sits far below the flight median ( z i < − 2 z_{i}<-2 ), and its size gap to the next-smallest individual exceeds twice the interquartile range of the flight’s areas. The second condition keeps the rule from firing on an adult that is merely the smallest of its herd ( Sec. 5 ).

sections.text: When an animal leaves the field of view and returns it is tracked afresh, so a census must recognize it across tracks without double-counting. This is narrower than re-identification in its usual sense: we match an animal to itself inside one flight, over minutes rather than seasons, against at most a dozen candidates and a nearly unchanged background. It is duplicate suppression for the census, not a general identity model, and the numbers below should be read that way. Every detection is geo-referenced ( Sec. 3.1 ), so a new track at ground position 𝐱 q \mathbf{x}_{q} is compared only against individuals last seen nearby, the candidate set 𝒩 q = { i : ∥ 𝐱 q − 𝐱 i ∥ 2 ≤ r } \mathcal{N}_{q}=\{i:\lVert\mathbf{x}_{q}-\mathbf{x}_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq r\} , with r r the distance the animal could plausibly have covered between sightings; an empty 𝒩 q \mathcal{N}_{q} means a new animal at no appearance cost. sections.heading: What cross-modal confirmation buys.
sections.text: Detection accuracy alone does not say how many of the resulting tracks are animals, which is what a census depends on. Table 2 answers that on the four census flights, holding 5802 5802 synchronized RGB–thermal frame pairs and 26 26 detectable individuals, none in any training set. The detectors produce 94 94 raw tracks between them, 43 43 in RGB and 51 51 in thermal. Requiring the modalities to agree accepts 30 30 , every one of which belongs to a ground-truth individual, registering tightly at median inter-center distances of 0.8 to 9.1 0.89.1 px inside the 28 28 px gate. Of the 34 34 tracks without a partner only one is a real animal, the male A1 R8, whom thermal never picks up and whom the length-and-confidence fallback correctly admits. That fallback is not reliable alone: applied uniformly it would admit six more tracks that no ground-truth animal accounts for, five on C , where dense canopy yields long, confident single-modality tracks on background structure.

On held-out tracks, balanced accuracy is 72 % 72\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} for RGB, 70 % 70\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} for thermal and 78 % 78\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} combined ( Tab. 3 ). These are moderate numbers, because occlusion is a hard and partly subjective call and 72 % 72\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of frames are clear. Filtering also removes frames, so the two blocks are scored on different numbers of crops and are read for direction rather than exact magnitude.

All eleven match the field ground truth: males D4 ( 106 106 / 115 115 ), D10 ( 145 145 / 157 157 ), D11 ( 109 109 / 150 150 ), and the size-flagged juvenile D5. D10 is the fusion-recovery case, both single modalities voting female (RGB 17 17 / 157 157 , thermal 59 59 / 157 157 ). No female is over-called, not even D6 ( 24 24 / 93 93 ). D12 is never detected. On top of species we classify sex ( male vs female / juvenile ) on red deer. The three DINOv3 heads are trained once , on the three-annotator consensus set ( Sec. 3.1 ), then evaluated frozen on the four held-out flights, each animal aggregated by majority vote over its non-occluded frames: one classifier and one rule, scored once per flight. The result is decided per individual. The combined head calls all 18 18 female / juvenile individuals correctly, that is 16 16 adult females and both juveniles, plus seven of the eight adult males, missing only A1 D4; either sensor alone recovers just two of the eight. Fusion wins because the single-modality failures are complementary ( Tab. 5 ): on two males the antler cue survives only in RGB, on two others only in thermal, and on three males both vote female yet the combined head still recovers male ( Fig. 5 ). Those last three are the informative cases: recovering them needs the joint representation itself, so fusion buys more here than any late combination of the two outputs could. Figure 3 shows the clearest crop of each male. Which sensor carries a male follows the antler cycle, and so the acquisition date: velvet antlers are vascularized and thermally hot and light up the thermal view, but once the velvet is shed the hardened antler goes thermally dead and only RGB resolves it [ 30 , 22 ] . The flights span the cycle, from summer velvet (B 2023-07-27, C 2026-06-25, A2 2026-06-26) to autumn hardened antler (A1 2023-09-20), so the modality carrying sex is intermittent while the fused view stays reliable. On C , canopy cover and a later fly-back over the same ground split the five individuals into thirteen raw tracks, eleven on D5, D2 and D1. Re-identification stitches these back across eight re-entries ( Fig. 4 ); the returners have moved, so appearance rather than position matches them. That keeps the single male from being counted as several animals and pools his scattered frames, so the intermittent cue still suffices to sex him.

sections.heading: 4.5 Size and the juvenile
sections.text: Figure 6 : Per-individual thermal box areas, perspective (left) and orthorectified (right), sorted by median size, filled by field ground truth and sharing identity labels across domains. male and female overlap over the whole range, so box area is a life-stage cue, not a sex cue. Hatching marks an incorrect sex call, one in perspective and three after orthorectification, each a male read as female . Grey slots are individuals missed in that domain (A1 D8 from its RGB box). Figure 7 : Orthographic thermal box areas for the two flights containing a juvenile, A2 and B , on a shared axis, filled by field ground truth; hatching marks an incorrect sex call. Within each flight the juvenile (orange) is the clear low outlier ( 0.53 × 0.53\times and 0.60 × 0.60\times the flight-cohort median), yet the B juvenile’s box ( ∼ 673 \sim\!673 px 2 ) still lands in A2 ’s female range, its detections carrying looser padding. Two of the four flights contain a juvenile, and the box-area outlier test flags each cleanly. The smallest animal is D5 on A2 and D2 on B ; each sits far below its own flight cohort, at 0.32 × 0.32\times and 0.60 × 0.60\times the cohort median in the native view, with Cohen’s d > 3 d>3 [ 8 ] and no adult close to it in size, and field ground truth confirms both as juveniles. A1 and C hold no such outlier, their smallest animals lying on a smooth size continuum, so the test does not over-fire. Orthographic size is also metric , so it should in principle compare across flights and altitudes. That does not yet hold: on B the thermal signal sits on a noisier background and the boxes are visibly looser, so the B juvenile’s box ( ∼ 673 \sim\!673 px 2 ) drifts up into the female range of A2 even though it is the smallest animal in its own flight ( Figs. 6 and 7 ). Loose-versus-tight box variation carries straight into the metric size ( Sec. 5 ), so we read life stage per flight rather than from one global threshold, and leave the cross-flight metric as work in progress.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: We turn dual-stream UAV video of red deer herds into an individual-level demographic census by fusing RGB and thermal at every stage, and which modality to trust proves situational. Thermal is the better detector and the only view surviving cast shadow, yet it confuses the small roe deer with red deer ( 7.7 % 7.7\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} species accuracy) and its sex accuracy swings from 37 % 37\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} to 91 % 91\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} with the environment; RGB carries the antler cue but loses shaded animals. Alone, each recovers only two of the eight males the fused head resolves to seven. Selecting frames rather than rejecting animals keeps that call clean; a box-size biometric supplies the life stage appearance cannot.

sections.heading: Beyond axis-aligned boxes.
sections.text: The geometric cue, box area as a life-stage proxy, rests on an axis-aligned box. A deer seen from above is elongated and lies at an arbitrary heading, so a diagonally oriented animal forces the box to include more background than an axis-parallel one, and the area varies with orientation as much as with body size. That weakens the juvenile-to-adult separation and feeds heading-dependent background into crops. Oriented boxes would give tighter, pose-aligned footprints [ 37 , 10 ] , and a head–tail keypoint pair would estimate orientation and length directly [ 24 , 38 ] ; orthorectified, that distance is a metric size cue that also flags curled or foreshortened frames. That is the clearest next step.

sections.heading: Remaining limitations.
sections.text: Three limitations remain. DINOv3 is not discriminative enough for individual aerial deer without mean-centering, and only the strongest re-identification pairs survive. Males are rare enough to leave single-modality heads prone to minority errors. And two animals sit near the boundary: the male A2 D10, whom only fusion recovers, and the female C D1 lying down, whose splayed posture reads as faintly male in the joint embedding ( 46 % 46\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} ) although both single modalities call her correctly.

sections.heading: What this changes for aerial surveys.
sections.text: A drone flight today may return a count, and the demographic reading that management acts on is added afterwards by hand, on a subsample of flights or not at all. Automating it lets composition be read on every flight, which is the frequency at which sex ratios and age structure stop being an occasional estimate and become trend data, and every call stays auditable in the frames and the vote behind it. What a survey reports changes with it: not one population number but a list of individuals, each with a species, a sex, a life stage and a confidence that a manager can question and carry into a population model. Red deer are an unusually legible case, so what transfers is the design rather than these accuracies: a demographic label is better taken as a decision over a track and two sensors than over one crop, and the evidence for it is seasonal, so a pipeline committed to one sensor will fail at some point in the year. Schedl Affiliation: University of Applied Sciences Upper Austria, Hagenberg, Austria Abstract Aerial drone surveys increasingly support wildlife population estimation, yet a useful census is more than a count: population dynamics are defined by species composition, sex ratios and age structure, that is, by which species are present and how a herd splits into adult males, adult females and juveniles. We use red deer ( Cervus elaphus ) as a test case, because managers act on these dynamics and because the visible cue defining adult males, the antlers, is seasonally variable. Surveys are flown nadir, the cameras looking straight down while the drone flies high enough not to disturb the animals, so each deer occupies only a small, low-resolution patch. The two recording modalities fail in opposite conditions: in color a deer under canopy blends into the ground, while in thermal it becomes a bright blob that loses fine detail. Rather than trust either modality alone, we fuse them at every stage using self-supervised DINOv3 features. Our pipeline tracks animals in both modalities, treats an animal as confirmed only when the two cameras agree, keeps only the clear, non-occluded frames, and assigns species and sex by a vote across them; life stage is read separately from geo-referenced body size, since at survey resolution a juvenile often only differs from an adult female in size. Across four flights spanning the antler season the fused pipeline correctly classifies 25 of the 26 detected individuals (7 of 8 adult males, all 16 adult females and 2 juveniles), against 20 of 26 for either sensor alone. The multimodal species classification reaches 96.0 % 96.0\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} , while for the sex classification, the fusion of the two sensors matters most: the combined RGB+thermal model is the most robust across environments and seasons. Automating the demographic classification turns a drone flight from a count into a repeatable reading of herd structure, so the sex ratios and age structure that managers already act on can be gathered as often as a survey can be flown. Keywords: Wildlife monitoring Multimodal fusion RGB–thermal Selective prediction Re-identification Demographic classification * * footnotetext: Corresponding authors (equal contribution): Hugo Markoff (khbm@bio.aau.dk), Christoph Praschl (christoph.praschl@fh-hagenberg.at) 1 Introduction Wildlife management needs to know not merely how many animals are present but which animals: how a population divides into adult males, adult females and juveniles. A survey reads that composition as a snapshot, the age and sex structure from which recruitment, survival and population trend are afterwards estimated [ 7 ] , yet it is exactly what detection and counting models do not report. We study the problem on red deer ( Cervus elaphus ), where the male/female/juvenile split is a standard management variable and the cues are unusually well defined from above: adult males carry antlers and adult females do not, while juveniles can look like small adult females and are difficult to tell apart by appearance at survey resolution. Uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) make repeated, low-disturbance surveys practical [ 13 , 9 ] , and pairing an RGB with a thermal camera is attractive in forest habitats, where animals slip in and out of canopy and its shadow. The two modalities fail in opposite conditions: in RGB a deer in cast shadow or under a crown is almost indistinguishable from the background, while in thermal it is an unmistakable bright blob but fur color is lost and antlers are visible only seasonally, limited by low resolution and warm-ground clutter. Figure 1 shows both failures, and which sensor performs better depends on the time of year: in June the velvet antlers are still warm and resolve in thermal, while by September they have hardened and gone thermally dark, so the cue survives only in RGB. Figure 1 : Why one modality is not enough, and why it is seasonal. One test area, two flights, each an RGB | | thermal pair with the male enlarged. In A1 (September) the antlers have hardened and gone thermally dead, so the sex cue survives only faintly, and only in RGB. In A2 (June) deer resting in the shaded strip beside the barn are barely separable from the ground in RGB but bright in thermal, where the warm velvet antlers resolve. From rejecting cases to selecting frames. Prior work on the same data treated the demographic label as a question of ecological evidence as much as of modeling: on small, occluded nadir crops the sex cue is often simply absent from a given view, so the response is to abstain rather than guess [ 23 ] . It also showed that heads built on pretrained foundation-model representations beat smaller specialized architectures such as YOLO, whose weaker capacity struggles with the faint cues of aerial imagery. Abstaining matters because forcing ambiguous crops into a class injects label noise that corrupts the classifier [ 28 , 12 ] , and clean supervision here is usually bought through active learning and review [ 19 , 20 ] . But abstention has a price: rejected crops are often ambiguous animals, and a census cannot discard its hard cases. In video an animal is not one crop but a track of many frames across the two modalities, so we reject the frames on which the evidence is absent or limited and settle sex and life stage by voting over the survivors, which keeps the clean-label benefit without losing the individuals abstention would discard. No single modality and no single frame is therefore enough for an individual-level census, yet almost all aerial wildlife pipelines stop at detection, counting or coarse tracking and leave the demographic step to manual review. We close that gap for one species as a demonstration that the step can be automated at all. The work extends a thermal-only localization and tracking pipeline [ 32 ] from one thermal stream to paired RGB–thermal detection and cross-modal tracking, from the native camera perspective to terrain-orthorectified imagery, and from localization to demographic classification. On the public BAMBI dataset ( Sec. 3.1 ) we contribute a pipeline that fuses the sensors at every stage and outputs, per individual, a species, a sex call, a life-stage flag and an occlusion-aware confidence, rendered onto the tracked video. Scope and questions. Four questions run through what follows. (i) What does cross-modal confirmation buy when deciding which tracks are animals and which are sensor noise ( Secs. 3.2 and 2 )? (ii) Which modality carries the sex signal ( Secs. 3.3 and 5 )? (iii) Does selecting frames rather than classifying all of them sharpen the census ( Secs. 3.3 and 4 )? (iv) How reliable is a box-derived size cue as a life-stage biometric, and what limits it ( Secs. 3.3 and 5 )? 2 Related Work 2.1 Aerial wildlife datasets and fine-grained interpretation Two things separate our setting from most airborne wildlife work: the habitat is forested rather than open, and the output is a demographic profile rather than a count. Airborne monitoring has mostly been developed for open habitats, where animals are comparatively visible and RGB alone often suffices for localization, counting and tracking [ 13 , 9 , 27 ] . Recent methods cut annotation effort further by learning density-based localization from points rather than boxes [ 5 ] , but do not recover the extent, orientation or appearance that individual tracking and demographic analysis need. Under canopy, RGB–thermal fusion improves robustness [ 2 , 21 ] , and thermal UAV surveys support red deer counting [ 39 ] and antler-based sex-ratio estimation [ 16 ] . All of these return aggregate quantities: a count for a flight, or a single ratio for a herd. None attaches a species, a sex and a life stage to an individual animal, and it is that step, from a population-level summary to a per-animal record, that we take here. 2.2 Tracking and re-identification Online trackers of the SORT family [ 1 ] pair a constant-velocity Kalman filter [ 18 ] with greedy association and remain a strong, simple baseline for aerial video. Appearance re-identification increasingly rests on self-supervised features: DINOv2 and DINOv3 [ 29 , 35 ] give transferable descriptors without labels, which triplet metric learning [ 34 , 15 ] can sharpen for identity and attribute discrimination. In ecology such metric learning underpins animal photo-identification [ 25 ] , though careful evaluation is needed to separate real gains from tuning artifacts [ 26 ] . Tracking alone does not scale to a survey: stitchers assume a static landscape, so animals that move during a flight are duplicated or ghosted in the orthomosaic and bias the count, which is why removing duplicates by distinguishing individuals is named an open direction [ 3 ] , while thermal UAV work on ungulates stops at detection and counting [ 31 , 39 ] . Aerial re-identification is usually approached from a lateral view, at least for species whose markings sit on the flank: Sun et al . [ 36 ] pair YOLOv11 with a DINOv2 pose classifier but maneuver the drone around each animal to expose it. Of the 53 53 datasets in WildlifeDatasets / MegaDescriptor [ 4 ] only AerialCattle2017 uses nadir views, because for cattle their coat pattern makes them separable. Red deer carry no such marking apart from the males’ antlers, which makes nadir re-identification harder. 2.3 Selective prediction and frame quality When evidence is weak it is often better to abstain than to force a label; selective classification formalizes this reject option [ 6 , 11 ] , and modern variants pair a classifier with a confidence estimate that decides when to defer [ 12 , 14 ] . These are general formulations rather than wildlife methods; the one treatment on aerial wildlife imagery we know of is the prior work on this same red deer data [ 23 ] . Here the analogous decision is which frames to classify at all , since an occluded or badly posed crop carries no reliable demographic evidence, and forcing it into a class injects label noise [ 28 ] . That work abstains per frame; we move the principle to the track level ( Sec. 3.3 ). 3 Method 3.1 Data and evaluation protocol We use the matched and orthographic subsets of the public BAMBI dataset [ 33 ] ( https://github.com/bambi-eco/Dataset ): paired, undistorted RGB–thermal recordings from temperate Austrian forests and forest edges, flown nadir with DJI M3T/M30T drones at 30 m to 60 m 30\text{\,}\mathrm{m}60\text{\,}\mathrm{m} above ground. RTK multi-GNSS gives centimeter-level per-frame pose, so each frame can be used in the native camera perspective or re-projected onto the terrain as an orthophoto (“geo”), in which detections carry world coordinates. The dataset ships bounding-box tracks , each with a species and, where identifiable, sex and age, plus an occlusion flag on the key frames. Red deer ( Cervus elaphus ) is the richest demographic class: 1613 1613 tracks and 26 674 26\,674 key frames, with sex annotated on 41.0 % 41.0\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of tracks, age on 67.6 % 67.6\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} and an occlusion flag on 49.5 % 49.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of key frames. Tracks and frames without a given label are unused by the corresponding head. Three supervision sources. Species labels come from a multi-species crop set ( 653 653 roe deer, 6868 6868 red deer, 4698 4698 wild boar paired crops). Occlusion labels are the per-key-frame visibility flags, giving 20 531 20\,531 labeled crops ( 14 744 14\,744 clear, 5787 5787 occluded). Sex follows the strictest protocol: every matched crop was re-reviewed independently by three annotators free to abstain, and only the 3908 3908 crops on which a majority agreed ( 556 556 male, 3352 3352 female/juvenile) were kept, so the sex head trains on a consensus-filtered set spanning the 2023–2024 antler cycle [ 23 ] , available at https://zenodo.org/records/21061638 . Classification heads are evaluated leakage-free with GroupKFold by animal track . These are the flights for which we hold field-verified demographic ground truth, so a per-individual census can be scored against what was present. Each census comes from one flight alone, and we do not link individuals across flights. Species is predicted for every detected animal; sex and life stage only for red deer, the one class with enough demographic annotation to support them. 3.2 Detection and cross-modal tracking Figure 2 gives the overall flow: the synchronized RGB and thermal (TH) streams are detected, tracked and cropped, then passed through a hierarchical classifier whose species and demographic stages run only on the frames an occlusion filter keeps. Loose-versus-tight box variation carries straight into the metric size ( Sec. 5 ), so we read life stage per flight rather than from one global threshold, and leave the cross-flight metric as work in progress. 5 Discussion and Conclusion We turn dual-stream UAV video of red deer herds into an individual-level demographic census by fusing RGB and thermal at every stage, and which modality to trust proves situational. Thermal is the better detector and the only view surviving cast shadow, yet it confuses the small roe deer with red deer ( 7.7 % 7.7\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} species accuracy) and its sex accuracy swings from 37 % 37\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} to 91 % 91\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} with the environment; RGB carries the antler cue but loses shaded animals. Alone, each recovers only two of the eight males the fused head resolves to seven. Selecting frames rather than rejecting animals keeps that call clean; a box-size biometric supplies the life stage appearance cannot. Beyond axis-aligned boxes. The geometric cue, box area as a life-stage proxy, rests on an axis-aligned box. A deer seen from above is elongated and lies at an arbitrary heading, so a diagonally oriented animal forces the box to include more background than an axis-parallel one, and the area varies with orientation as much as with body size. That weakens the juvenile-to-adult separation and feeds heading-dependent background into crops. Oriented boxes would give tighter, pose-aligned footprints [ 37 , 10 ] , and a head–tail keypoint pair would estimate orientation and length directly [ 24 , 38 ] ; orthorectified, that distance is a metric size cue that also flags curled or foreshortened frames. That is the clearest next step. Remaining limitations. Three limitations remain. DINOv3 is not discriminative enough for individual aerial deer without mean-centering, and only the strongest re-identification pairs survive. Males are rare enough to leave single-modality heads prone to minority errors. And two animals sit near the boundary: the male A2 D10, whom only fusion recovers, and the female C D1 lying down, whose splayed posture reads as faintly male in the joint embedding ( 46 % 46\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} ) although both single modalities call her correctly. What this changes for aerial surveys. A drone flight today may return a count, and the demographic reading that management acts on is added afterwards by hand, on a subsample of flights or not at all. Automating it lets composition be read on every flight, which is the frequency at which sex ratios and age structure stop being an occasional estimate and become trend data, and every call stays auditable in the frames and the vote behind it. What a survey reports changes with it: not one population number but a list of individuals, each with a species, a sex, a life stage and a confidence that a manager can question and carry into a population model. Red deer are an unusually legible case, so what transfers is the design rather than these accuracies: a demographic label is better taken as a decision over a track and two sensors than over one crop, and the evidence for it is seasonal, so a pipeline committed to one sensor will fail at some point in the year.
